title: The procurement strategy
blurb: Explain what a procurement strategy is for, why it matters and what it typically contains.
question: A council is about to refurbish a library and will buy building work, furniture and a new IT system from outside suppliers. The sponsor asks why the project manager wants to write a procurement strategy before contacting any suppliers, and what it will cover. How should the project manager answer?

teach.h: Decide how to buy before you buy
teach.body: A procurement strategy is the high-level approach for securing the goods and services a project needs from external suppliers. In plain English: before anyone talks to a supplier, it decides what you will buy, how you will find and choose suppliers, how you will contract with and pay them, and how risk will be shared. It is written early, while the project is being defined, so that buying serves the project's objectives instead of happening ad hoc.

children.label: Value for money
children.sub: Best whole-life value, not just the lowest price

children.label: Supply-chain risk
children.sub: Risks spotted and placed with the right party

children.label: Quality & timely supply
children.sub: Right standard, arriving when the plan needs it

children.label: Alignment
children.sub: Buying decisions serve the project's needs

teach.caption: These five purposes are what a strong written answer on 'importance' draws on.

teach.body: Without a strategy, each purchase is made in isolation. Typical results: materials ordered too late and hitting the critical path, premium prices paid under time pressure, contracts that overlap or leave gaps, risks landing with whoever happened to sign last, and, in the public sector, a legal challenge because the competition was not run fairly. A strategy turns buying into a planned, joined-up activity that is agreed by governance before money is committed.

teach.h: Typical contents of a procurement strategy
head: Typical content
The question it answers
rows: Do it in-house or buy it in?
One supplier, several, or a framework?
Who can supply, at what price and risk?
What will the contract look like?
How will suppliers be managed after award?
teach.caption: A typical list. Turn each row into a question and you can rebuild the whole strategy in an exam.

teach.h: The first decision: make or buy?

root.label: Make or buy?
root.sub: Can we do it ourselves, or should we buy it in?

children.label: In-house
children.sub: More control, keeps know-how, uses spare capacity

children.label: External supplier
children.sub: Specialist skills, extra capacity, speed, risk shared

teach.caption: Only what you decide to buy needs the rest of the strategy: sourcing, selection, contract and payment.
The strategy comes first and shapes every later step. It typically sits alongside, or within, the project management plan.

teach.h: Linear versus iterative: how the strategy differs

rows.label: Pricing
values: Per time box or cost based

teach.caption: Tendencies, not rules. Iterative work is harder to contract because the total scope is not known up front.

teach.body: Harbourside Council is refurbishing its library. Its strategy decides that council staff will write the design brief (make), building works go to one main contractor on a fixed price because the design is complete, furniture is called off from an existing framework, and the self-service IT system comes from a specialist. Evaluation criteria weigh quality and social value alongside price, the timetable allows for public procurement rules, and the sponsor approves contracts above the project manager's limit.

teach.text: Classic trap: the procurement strategy is the high-level APPROACH. It is not the contract, not the tender documents and not the selection process itself. Value for money is not 'lowest price': quality, whole-life cost and risk count too. In 'which is NOT part of a procurement strategy' questions, the odd one out is usually something internal to the team (team building, holiday rotas, office layout).

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define it: the high-level approach for securing goods and services from external suppliers.
Give a purpose and say WHY: value for money, so the project gets the best whole-life value, not just a low price.
Add risk: it identifies supply-chain risks and places each with the party best able to manage it.
Add compliance and timing: it keeps buying within rules (e.g. public procurement) and on time for the schedule.
For 'contents' questions, name specific items (make or buy, sourcing, criteria, reimbursement, risk allocation) and tie each to the scenario.
A procurement strategy is the high-level approach for securing goods and services from external suppliers.
Purposes: value for money, supply-chain risk, quality, timely supply, compliance, alignment with project needs.
Typical contents: make or buy, sourcing, market analysis, criteria, contract, reimbursement, risk, timescales, roles, contract management.
Iterative projects usually need more flexible pricing and a more collaborative relationship.
It is not the contract or the tender pack: it shapes both.

summary: You can now explain what a procurement strategy is and why it matters: value for money, supply-chain risk, quality, timely supply and compliance. You can also list its typical contents and show how it changes for an iterative project.

A.q: Which statement best describes a procurement strategy?
options: The signed agreement setting each supplier's duties
The high-level approach to securing external supply
The tender pack sent out to invite supplier bids
The register of suppliers the organisation trusts
A.why: A procurement strategy is the high-level approach for securing the goods and services a project needs from external suppliers.

whyNot.0: That is the contract, which the strategy leads to but is not the same thing.
whyNot.2: Tender documents (ITT, RFP or RFQ) are produced later, during supplier selection, following the strategy.
whyNot.3: An approved supplier list may be used by a strategy, but it is not the strategy itself.

A.q: A construction firm's sponsor asks why the project needs a procurement strategy at all. Which is the BEST reason?
options: It guarantees that the cheapest bid is accepted
It replaces the need for a project risk register
It transfers all of the project's risk to suppliers
It secures value for money and manages supply risk
A.why: A procurement strategy aims for value for money and manages supply-chain risk, as well as quality, timely supply and compliance.

whyNot.0: Value for money is not the same as the lowest price: quality, risk and whole-life cost matter too.
whyNot.1: Procurement risks feed into the project's risk management; the strategy does not replace the risk register.
whyNot.2: A strategy places each risk with the party best able to manage it; it does not push every risk onto suppliers.

A.q: Which of the following would NOT normally appear in a procurement strategy?
options: Team-building activities for the project team
The criteria for selecting and evaluating suppliers
How risk will be allocated between the parties
The method that will be used to pay the suppliers
A.why: Team building is about developing the project team, not about how goods and services will be bought.

whyNot.1: Selection and evaluation criteria are a typical content of a procurement strategy.
whyNot.2: Risk allocation between buyer and supplier is a typical content.
whyNot.3: The reimbursement (payment) method is a typical content.

B.q: A water company could use its own engineers to design a new treatment works or hire a specialist consultancy. Which part of the procurement strategy addresses this choice?
options: The contract management plan
The reimbursement method
The make-or-buy decision
The bidder debrief process
B.why: Make or buy decides whether work is done in-house or bought from an external supplier.

whyNot.0: Contract management covers how suppliers are managed after the contract is awarded.
whyNot.1: The reimbursement method covers how a supplier is paid, once you have decided to buy.
whyNot.3: Debriefing unsuccessful bidders is a step in supplier selection, not a decision about whether to buy.

B.q:
Which THREE of the following are typical contents of a procurement strategy?
1) The sourcing approach (e.g. single supplier or framework)
2) Timescales for the procurement
3) The project team's holiday rota
4) Roles and governance for buying decisions
options: 1, 2 and 4
1, 2 and 3
1, 3 and 4
2, 3 and 4
B.why: Sourcing approach, timescales, and roles and governance are all typical contents. A holiday rota is internal team admin.

whyNot.1: Item 3, the holiday rota, is team admin and not part of a procurement strategy.
whyNot.2: Item 3, the holiday rota, does not belong in a procurement strategy.
whyNot.3: Item 3 is wrong, and this option leaves out the sourcing approach, a core content.

B.q: An events company ran a festival with no procurement strategy. Staging was booked late from whichever firm was free, at a premium, and two contracts overlapped. What would a strategy MOST have provided?
options: A faster way to approve the business case
A guarantee that no supplier would fail
A replacement for the event's schedule
A planned, joined-up approach to buying
B.why: A strategy plans what to buy, when and how, so purchases are timely, coordinated and good value instead of ad hoc.

whyNot.0: The business case justifies the project; the procurement strategy does not speed up its approval.
whyNot.1: No strategy can guarantee supplier performance; it manages supply-chain risk rather than removing it.
whyNot.2: Procurement timescales feed into the schedule; the strategy does not replace it.

C.q: A fintech firm will build a mobile app iteratively with an external development agency. Requirements will emerge sprint by sprint. What should the procurement strategy MOST likely favour?
options: One lump-sum price for a full, frozen specification
A collaborative relationship with flexible scope
Choosing the agency purely on its lowest day rate
Holding back all supplier input until handover
C.why: In iterative work, scope flexes, so a single fixed price for a frozen specification is hard to set. The strategy should favour collaboration and payment that lets scope change (for example per time box, or cost based).

whyNot.0: A lump sum needs a well-defined, stable scope, which iterative work does not have up front.
whyNot.2: Value for money weighs capability, quality and risk, not just the day rate.
whyNot.3: In iterative delivery the supplier works with users in every iteration, not just at the end.

C.q: A government agency plans to buy a case management system worth several million pounds. Which consideration is MOST critical for its procurement strategy to address?
options: Choosing suppliers the team already knows
Keeping the requirement hidden from bidders
Complying with public procurement rules
Agreeing a price before defining the need
C.why: Public bodies must follow public procurement rules for fair, open and transparent competition. Compliance is one of the strategy's key purposes.

whyNot.0: Favouring familiar suppliers risks breaching fair-competition rules and may not give best value.
whyNot.1: Bidders need a clear requirement to price against; hiding it would undermine the competition.
whyNot.3: The need must be defined first; the price comes out of the competition.

C.q: Ground conditions on a tunnel project are highly uncertain. The procurement strategy proposes that the client keeps this risk rather than passing it to the contractor. What is the MAIN reasoning?
options: Risk should sit with whoever can best manage it
Suppliers are never allowed to carry any risk
Clients always pay less when holding every risk
Risk allocation is settled after the work ends
C.why: Risk should be placed with the party best able to manage or bear it. A contractor forced to take an unknowable risk would price in a large premium, which is poor value.

whyNot.1: Suppliers often carry risk, for example cost risk under a fixed price.
whyNot.2: Holding risk is not automatically cheaper; if the risk happens, the client pays. The aim is best value.
whyNot.3: Risk allocation is decided in the strategy and fixed in the contract before work starts.

reteach.title: Planning a kitchen refit
reteach.question: Before you ring a single kitchen company, you make some decisions about how you will get the work done. How do those decisions mirror a procurement strategy?

blocks.body: You decide to paint the walls yourself but buy in the fitting (make or buy). You choose whether one kitchen firm does everything or you hire a plumber, electrician and joiner separately (sourcing approach). You decide to get three quotes and read reviews (selection criteria), whether to pay a fixed quote or a day rate (reimbursement), who pays if the old pipes are rotten (risk allocation), and when it must be done by (timescales).

head: Kitchen decision
Strategy content
rows: Paint it myself, buy in fitting

blocks.text: Notice that none of this is the job itself, the quotes or the signed agreement. The strategy is the thinking you do BEFORE you go to market, and it shapes everything that follows.

explain.body: The procurement strategy is the high-level approach for securing the goods and services a project needs from external suppliers. It comes before supplier selection and shapes the contract.

test.q: Complete the statement: a procurement strategy sets out the ___ for securing goods and services from external suppliers.
options: detailed daily tasks
signed legal terms
final invoice totals
high-level approach
test.why: It is the high-level approach for securing goods and services from external suppliers.

whyNot.0: Daily tasks belong in detailed schedules, not the strategy.
whyNot.1: Signed legal terms are the contract, which comes later.
whyNot.2: Invoice totals arise during contract management.

explain.body: It secures value for money (best whole-life value, not just lowest price), manages supply-chain risk, protects quality and timely supply, keeps buying compliant with rules such as public procurement, and aligns purchases with project needs.

test.q:
Which TWO are key purposes of a procurement strategy?
1) Achieving value for money
2) Avoiding the need for a business case
3) Managing supply-chain risk
4) Removing the need to evaluate bids
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
test.why: Value for money and managing supply-chain risk are both core purposes of a procurement strategy.

whyNot.0: A strategy never removes the need for a business case.
whyNot.2: Neither 2 nor 4 is a purpose: the business case and bid evaluation are still needed.
whyNot.3: Bids must still be evaluated, so item 4 is wrong.

explain.body: Make or buy, sourcing approach (single or multiple suppliers, framework), market analysis, selection and evaluation criteria, contract type and terms, reimbursement method, risk allocation, timescales, roles and governance, and the contract management approach.

test.q: A project manager records whether the work will go to one main contractor, several direct suppliers or an existing framework. Which typical content of the strategy is this?
options: Market analysis
Evaluation criteria
Sourcing approach
Contract management
test.why: The sourcing approach sets out how many suppliers will be used and how (single, multiple or via a framework).

whyNot.0: Market analysis studies who can supply and at what price and risk.
whyNot.1: Evaluation criteria set how bids will be judged.
whyNot.3: Contract management covers how suppliers are managed after award.

explain.body: The strategy is tailored to the market and the life cycle. Market analysis shows who can supply, their capacity and price trends. In a linear project with a fixed design, a fixed price may suit; in an iterative project, scope flexes, so pricing and relationships must be more flexible.

test.q: Before deciding how to buy, a team studies how many firms could deliver, their capacity and recent price trends. Which typical content of the strategy is this?
options: Market analysis
Risk allocation
Reimbursement method
Roles and governance
test.why: Market analysis looks at who can supply, their capacity, prices and risks, so the strategy is realistic.

whyNot.1: Risk allocation decides who carries which risks.
whyNot.2: The reimbursement method decides how suppliers will be paid.
whyNot.3: Roles and governance set who decides and approves.
